55436.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse sól (“sun”), from Proto-Germanic *sōl (“sun”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”). The exact inflectional prehistory of the Proto-Germanic form is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk sol, Danish sol, Swedish sol, Icelandic sól, Faroese sól, Latin sōl (“sun”) and English sun. / Borrowed from Italian sol (“sol, fifth note of the scale”), from the first syllable of Latin solve (“release, unbind”) in the medieval hymn Ut queant laxis. The note name belongs to the solmization system associated with Guido of Arezzo. / Shortened from Latin solūtiō (“solution”) (genitive solūtiōnis), originally used as an element in terms such as aerosol.
Compare German Sol, English sol and French sol (“colloidal solution”). / Clipping of solarium (“solarium, tanning bed”).

2444.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂epó
First attested in the by 1836.
a priori (“a priori”) + -isk (“adjective-forming suffix”).
The base, a priori (“a priori”), is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“from the former; from first principles”), literally “from the former”.
The first element, ā (“from”), is a form of ab (“from, away from”), inherited from Proto-Italic *ap (“from, away from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”).
The second element, priōrī, is the ablative singular of prior (“earlier, former, previous”), from Proto-Italic *priōs (“earlier, previous”), from earlier Proto-Italic

1000076.etyen:
Internationalism, based on the name of the island, which the Dutch named Mauritzeiland (“Maurits Island”) in 1598 after Maurits van Nassau, Prince of Orange and stadtholder of the Dutch Republic. The Dutch name consists of the personal name Maurits (“Maurice”) and eiland (“island”). The modern country subsequently took its name from the island.
The personal name Maurits continues Latin Mauritius (“Maurice”), an extension of Latin Maurus (“Moor; inhabitant of Mauretania”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Μαῦρος (Maûros, “Moor”). The ultimate origin of the Ancient Greek term is uncertain; one

1001356.etyen:
Variant of Kaspar, from Medieval Latin Caspar (“male given name”), traditionally the name of one of the Magi in Western Christianity. Usually explained as ultimately from Biblical Hebrew גִּזְבָּר (gizbar, “treasurer”), from Classical Syriac ܓܙܒܪܐ (gēzaḇrā, “treasurer”), from Old Persian *ganzabarah (“treasurer”), from Median. Doublet of Jesper (“male given name”).
First attested in the 15th century in Norway.
Compare Danish Kasper, Swedish Kasper, German Kaspar, Dutch Casper, English Caspar, French Gaspard, Spanish Gaspar and Polish Kacper (“male given name”).
